title: Acute Myocarditis: Recognition, Investigation and Cardiology Escalation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with suspected acute myocarditis in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition, exclusion of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), risk stratification, when to admit and when to refer to a centre able to give mechanical circulatory support and endomyocardial biopsy, and first-line medicines. Source is the 2025 ESC guideline, with US product labels for medicine details. Not for chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy, peripartum cardiomyopathy (separate topic), or children.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi myocarditis guideline was found; the pathway follows the 2025 ESC guideline written for Europe.

ESC 2025 says NSAIDs (with a proton pump inhibitor) should be considered for pericarditic symptoms and colchicine for myopericarditis but gives no dose in the myocarditis section; the doses used here are the pericarditis doses in ESC Table 13. Restricting ibuprofen to patients with preserved ejection fraction and no heart failure is taken from the ibuprofen label warning (avoid in severe heart failure), not from ESC.

ESC says to follow the ESC heart failure guideline for myocarditis with left ventricular dysfunction, but that guideline was not opened; only furosemide (label acute pulmonary oedema dose) and metoprolol succinate (label heart failure titration) are given, and other heart failure drugs are not listed.
The beta-blocker dose for arrhythmia prevention in acute myocarditis (ESC Recommendation Table 9) is not given by ESC; the metoprolol succinate dose is the label heart failure regimen.
Norepinephrine and dobutamine are not dosed in the ESC text; doses are from the US labels (norepinephrine 8 to 12 mcg/min start; dobutamine 0.5 to 1 mcg/kg/min start then 2 to 20 mcg/kg/min).

Methylprednisolone 7 to 14 mg/kg/day for 3 days (about 500 to 1000 mg/day for a 70 kg adult) is as printed in ESC Table 12; it is far above the label's usual doses and the label's 30 mg/kg high-dose regimen was not used.
The ESC text recommends corticosteroids only for selected, usually biopsy-proven, forms; ESC states they are not recommended in acute myocarditis with preserved left ventricular function.
Typical adult laboratory reference ranges are not taken from the guideline; laboratories differ.

pathophysiology.summary: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle, most often presumed viral (enteroviruses, adenoviruses, parvovirus B19, herpesviruses, influenza, coronaviruses) (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.1). It can also be immune-mediated, for example giant-cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid or immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.1 and Table 12). Acute myocarditis often recovers: in biopsy-proven cases up to 50% recover spontaneously, up to 25% have stable persistent dysfunction and 10% to 25% progress (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.1.3). Fulminant myocarditis causes cardiogenic shock and has higher rates of death and heart transplantation (ESC 2025, Section 4.2.2). Arrhythmias can be the presentation or a complication (ESC 2025, Section 4.3).
keyMechanisms: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle, most often presumed viral (enteroviruses, adenoviruses, parvovirus B19, herpesviruses, influenza, coronaviruses) (ESC 2025, Section 3.4.1).

symptoms: Infarct-like chest pain, often after a flu-like illness or gastroenteritis (ESC 2025, Table 6).
Heart failure symptoms: breathlessness, fatigue, oedema (ESC 2025, Table 6).
physicalSigns: Haemodynamic instability or cardiogenic shock (ESC 2025, Table 6 and Table 7).
Ventricular arrhythmia or atrioventricular block (ESC 2025, Table 6 and Table 7).
Signs of heart failure and, with pericardial involvement, a friction rub (ESC 2025, Table 6).
ECG changes and raised troponin (ESC 2025, Table 6).
redFlags: Acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Cardiac arrest, syncope, sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation, high-level atrioventricular block (ESC 2025, Table 7).
New left ventricular ejection fraction below 40% or extensive late gadolinium enhancement on cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Persistent or relapsing troponin release (intermediate risk) (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, eosinophilia or systemic autoimmune disease suggest a treatable specific cause (ESC 2025, Table 12 and Section 6.2.1).
precipitants: Recent viral illness (ESC 2025, Table 6 and Section 3.4.1).
Immune checkpoint inhibitor cancer therapy (ESC 2025, Table 12).
Infections including Lyme disease and Chagas disease (ESC 2025, Table 12); HIV and hepatitis C are the only viral serology tests recommended (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 1).
Autoimmune and hypereosinophilic conditions, sarcoidosis (ESC 2025, Table 12).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: ESC names ACS as the main differential diagnosis for myocarditis with infarct-like pain, troponin rise and ECG change; rule out obstructive coronary disease by coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography (CT) according to clinical likelihood (ESC 2025, Section 5 and Recommendation Table 1).
Pericarditic pain and troponin rise without new impairment of left ventricular function (ESC 2025, Section 8).

Gene variants for desmosomal or sarcomeric proteins can overlap with myocarditis and myocardial inflammation can occur in inherited cardiomyopathy such as arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy; recurrent or familial cases and sustained ventricular arrhythmia prompt genetic testing (ESC 2025, Section 5.3 and Recommendation Table 2).

differentials.condition: Cardiomyopathy or non-inflammatory acute heart failure
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute heart failure is worked up with the CHAMPIT approach and CMR or biopsy (ESC 2025, Figure 10).

clinicalManagement.title: Stabilise and exclude acute coronary syndrome
actions: Take history, examine, and do an ECG, transthoracic echocardiography, chest X-ray and blood tests including troponin and NT-proBNP (ESC 2025, Figure 5).
Rule out acute coronary syndrome (ACS) when indicated, with coronary angiography or coronary CT (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 1).
Admit to a ward or intensive care unit (ICU) if there are high-risk clinical features (ESC 2025, Figure 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Stratify risk
actions: Classify as high, intermediate or low risk with Table 7 (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Admit moderate- to high-risk myocarditis for monitoring and treatment (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 1).
Arrange CMR in stable patients (ESC 2025, Figure 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat cardiogenic shock and fulminant myocarditis
actions: Give vasopressor or inotropic support and refer urgently to a tertiary centre able to give temporary mechanical circulatory support and early endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.1.2).
Early EMB is linked to lower death or transplant or ventricular assist device at 1 year (ESC 2025, Section 6.2.1.2).
Consider corticosteroids in fulminant non-infectious forms (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat heart failure and arrhythmias
actions: Treat congestion with intravenous furosemide and follow the ESC heart failure guideline for left ventricular dysfunction (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).
Consider a beta-blocker for at least 6 months in acute myocarditis, especially with raised troponin, once not in shock (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).
Continue heart failure therapy for at least 6 months after full recovery of left ventricular function (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Manage chest pain with pericardial involvement
actions: Consider an NSAID with a proton pump inhibitor for pericarditic symptoms and colchicine for myopericarditis (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).
Do not give corticosteroids for acute myocarditis with preserved left ventricular function (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).

clinicalManagement.title: Discharge planning
actions: Restrict physical exercise until remission, for at least 1 month (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 27).
Arrange follow-up with clinical assessment, biomarkers, ECG, exercise test, rhythm monitoring, echocardiography and CMR (ESC 2025, Table 15).
Discuss high-risk cases in a multidisciplinary team at a referral centre (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 27).

regimens.patientGroup: Adults with myopericarditis, preserved ejection fraction
regimens.dose: 600 mg to 800 mg orally three times daily (ESC 2025, Table 13 pericarditis dose). Tablets are 600 mg and 800 mg (Ibuprofen label, Section Description). Preparation: none; take with food.
regimens.duration: Shortest course that controls pain; 1 to 2 weeks then taper by 200 mg every 1 to 2 weeks (ESC 2025, Table 13)
adjustments: Avoid in severe heart failure or reduced ejection fraction (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings: Heart Failure and Edema).
Avoid in advanced renal disease (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings: Advanced Renal Disease).
Give with a proton pump inhibitor (ESC 2025, Recommendation Table 9).

monitoring: Troponin, ejection fraction and blood pressure (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Creatinine and signs of gastrointestinal bleeding (Ibuprofen label, Section Warnings).
contraindications: Coronary artery bypass graft surgery setting (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).
Aspirin triad: asthma, rhinitis, nasal polyps with aspirin sensitivity (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).
Hypersensitivity to NSAIDs (Ibuprofen label, Section Contraindications).

regimens.indication: Hypotension in cardiogenic shock from fulminant myocarditis
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with cardiogenic shock from myocarditis
regimens.dose: Dilute one 4 mg/4 mL vial in 1000 mL of 5% dextrose to give 4 mcg/mL. Start 8 to 12 mcg/min by intravenous infusion, adjust to the blood pressure target; typical maintenance 2 to 4 mcg/min (Norepinephrine label, Section 2.2 and Section 2.3). Infuse into a large vein.
regimens.duration: Until haemodynamically stable or mechanical circulatory support is in place; reduce the rate gradually
adjustments: Correct hypovolaemia first (Norepinephrine label, Section 2.1).
Avoid leg veins in older people or those with occlusive vascular disease (Norepinephrine label, Section 2.1).
Extravasation: infiltrate the ischaemic area with 5 to 10 mg phentolamine in 10 to 15 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (Norepinephrine label, Section 5.1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Blood pressure every 2 minutes until at target, then every 5 minutes (Norepinephrine label, Section 2.2).
Infusion site for extravasation (Norepinephrine label, Section 5.1).
contraindications: None are listed in the label (Norepinephrine label, Section 4); correct hypovolaemia before starting (Norepinephrine label, Section 2.1 and Section 5.1).
Sulfite allergy: the product contains sodium metabisulfite (Norepinephrine label, Section 5.4).

regimens.indication: Low cardiac output in fulminant myocarditis

regimens.dose: Start 0.5 to 1 mcg/kg/min by intravenous infusion and titrate every few minutes to response; usual range 2 to 20 mcg/kg/min, rarely up to 40 mcg/kg/min (Dobutamine label, Section Dosage and Administration). regimens.duration: Shortest time needed; wean as perfusion recovers
adjustments: Cautious dose selection in older patients (Dobutamine label, Section Geriatric Use).

regimens.indication: Specific immunosuppression for severe non-infectious myocarditis
regimens.patientGroup: Adults with severe or fulminant non-infectious myocarditis, specialist-directed
regimens.dose: 7 to 14 mg/kg/day intravenously for 3 days (about 500 to 1000 mg/day in a 70 kg adult), then prednisone 1 mg/kg/day orally (ESC 2025, Table 12). Vials of 40, 125, 500 mg, 1 g and 2 g (Solu-Medrol label, Section How Supplied). Reconstitute with the supplied diluent or bacteriostatic water, then add to 5% dextrose, isotonic saline or 5% dextrose in saline for infusion. Do not give more than 0.5 g over less than 10 minutes (Solu-Medrol label, Section Dosage and Administration).
regimens.duration: 3 days, then oral prednisone with taper
adjustments: Avoid in systemic fungal infection (Solu-Medrol label, Section Contraindications).
Rapid large doses have caused arrhythmia and bradycardia: monitor the ECG (Solu-Medrol label, Section Dosage and Administration).
Immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis: stop the inhibitor; non-severe cases use methylprednisolone 500 to 1000 mg/day for 3 days (ESC 2025, Table 12).

branches.entryCriteria: Adult with myocarditis, ejection fraction below 50% or heart failure, systolic blood pressure maintained, no cardiogenic shock.

branches.label: Cardiogenic shock or fulminant myocarditis
branches.entryCriteria: Adult with myocarditis and cardiogenic shock (fulminant myocarditis) needing vasopressor or inotropic support.

branches.label: Biopsy-proven or specialist-directed immunosuppression (fulminant non-infectious, giant-cell, eosinophilic, sarcoid or immune checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis)
branches.entryCriteria: Adult with EMB-proven or specialist-diagnosed non-infectious myocarditis in whom immunosuppression is indicated (ESC 2025, Table 12 and Recommendation Table 9).

medicationPlan.note: Therapy follows ESC 2025 Recommendation Table 9 and Table 12. Doses are from the ESC tables where given and otherwise from US product labels. Specific immunosuppression is for specialist, biopsy-directed use. diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Clinical presentation (infarct-like pain, heart failure, arrhythmia or syncope) with CMR-proven or endomyocardial biopsy (EMB)-proven myocarditis (ESC 2025, Table 4).
Clinical presentation with at least one additional criterion (ECG, raised troponin or NT-proBNP, imaging abnormality) where CMR or EMB is uncertain or not available (ESC 2025, Table 4).
Clinical presentation only, with no additional criterion (ESC 2025, Table 4).

Acute heart failure or cardiogenic shock, refractory NYHA III to IV dyspnoea, cardiac arrest or syncope, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, high-level atrioventricular block, new ejection fraction below 40% or extensive late gadolinium enhancement (ESC 2025, Table 7).

New or progressive dyspnoea, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, persistent or relapsing troponin, ejection fraction 41% to 49% or wall motion abnormality, or preserved ejection fraction with late gadolinium enhancement in 2 or more segments (ESC 2025, Table 7).
Stable or few symptoms with preserved ejection fraction (50% or higher) and no or limited (under 2 segments) late gadolinium enhancement (ESC 2025, Table 7).

teaching.scope: Adults with suspected acute myocarditis in the emergency department (ED) or acute medical ward: recognition, exclusion of acute coronary syndrome (ACS), risk stratification, when to admit and when to refer to a centre able to give mechanical circulatory support and endomyocardial biopsy, and first-line medicines. Source is the 2025 ESC guideline, with US product labels for medicine details. Not for chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy, peripartum cardiomyopathy (separate topic), or children.
learningObjectives: Recognise myocarditis in a patient with chest pain, raised troponin and a viral prodrome.
Rule out ACS and stratify risk with Table 7.
Know when to refer for mechanical circulatory support and biopsy.
Know that most acute myocarditis is treated supportively.
pitfalls: Treating as ACS only and missing myocarditis.
Giving NSAIDs in patients with heart failure.
keyPoints: High-risk features need admission and a centre with mechanical circulatory support.
Corticosteroids are not for acute myocarditis with preserved function.
Beta-blockers are considered for at least 6 months but not in shock.
Restrict exercise for at least 1 month.

patientEducation: Myocarditis is inflammation of the heart muscle, often after a viral illness, and many people recover fully.
Do not do strenuous exercise or sport for at least 1 month, until your cardiologist says it is safe.
Take heart tablets as prescribed and do not stop beta-blockers suddenly.
Return urgently for chest pain, fainting, palpitations or worsening breathlessness.
lifestyleAndDiet: No competitive or strenuous exercise until cleared, at least 1 month.
Avoid alcohol while the heart is recovering.
Attend all cardiology reviews and scans.
mdtReferrals: Emergency physician; cardiologist and heart failure team; critical care and mechanical support team; cardiac imaging; pathology for biopsy; pharmacist; rehabilitation.
dischargeCriteria: Haemodynamically stable; troponin falling; no ventricular arrhythmia on monitoring; ejection fraction known; medicines and exercise restriction explained; cardiology and imaging follow-up booked (ESC 2025, Table 15).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review with clinical assessment, biomarkers, ECG, exercise test, rhythm monitoring, echocardiography and CMR as in ESC Table 15; continue heart failure therapy for at least 6 months after recovery; no exercise for at least 1 month (ESC 2025, Table 15 and Recommendation Table 27).
